nameStory: The Meadow Dark-eyed Orbweaver gets its name from its preference for open grassy areas and meadows, combined with its distinctively dark eye region. The 'orbweaver' part refers to the classic round, wheel-like webs these spiders construct, with sticky spiral threads radiating out from the center like spokes.
description: The Meadow Dark-eyed Orbweaver is a small to medium-sized spider that builds the classic circular webs we often picture when thinking of spider webs. These spiders have a compact, rounded abdomen and are typically brown or grayish in color with darker markings around their eye area. They're part of the large orbweaver family, known for their geometric web-building skills and their habit of sitting in the center of their webs waiting for prey.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Dark coloration around the eye region gives this spider its distinctive 'dark-eyed' appearance, contrasting with lighter body colors

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic circular orb webs with neat, evenly-spaced spiral threads that feel sticky to the touch when accidentally walked into

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, rounded abdomen that feels firm when gently observed, with relatively short legs compared to some other orbweavers

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brown or gray coloration with subtle darker patterns on the abdomen, often with a somewhat mottled appearance

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web during daylight hours, quickly dropping or running to web edges when disturbed

habitat: Look for Meadow Dark-eyed Orbweavers in open grassy areas, meadows, and field edges throughout New England. They prefer sunny locations with adequate vegetation to anchor their webs, often building between tall grasses or low shrubs. You'll typically find them in areas with good insect activity to support their web-based hunting strategy.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing and building webs as insects become more active. Look for fresh, perfectly constructed orb webs in meadow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with mature spiders maintaining webs and mating. This is the best time to observe their classic web-building behavior.
seasonality.fall: Females may be seen with egg sacs, and spider activity continues until first hard frosts. Webs become more visible with morning dew.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, with the next generation overwintering as eggs or young spiders in protected locations.

funFact: Despite being called 'dark-eyed,' this spider's eyes themselves aren't actually dark - it's the surrounding facial area that's darker, creating a kind of natural 'eye shadow' effect that makes the spider look like it's wearing sunglasses!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small orbweavers in meadow habitats. The key distinguishing feature is the dark coloration specifically around the eye area - other orbweavers may be similarly sized and colored but lack this distinctive 'masked' appearance around the face.
contextualKnowledge: This species has been documented only once in New England according to current records, making it quite rare in our region. If you think you've spotted one, it would be worth photographing for verification, as it could represent an important regional sighting.
compareHints: The Meadow Dark-eyed Orbweaver differs from its close relative, the Rubens Orbweaver, primarily in coloration and habitat preference. While both are small orbweavers, the Meadow species has the characteristic dark eye region and prefers open grassy areas, whereas the Rubens Orbweaver typically has different coloration patterns and may be found in different microhabitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Rubens Orbweaver differs from its close relative, the Meadow Dark-eyed Orbweaver, primarily through its warmer reddish-brown tones versus the latter's darker, more muted coloration.
